chief_complaint: severe watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and high fever following clindamycin antibiotic course
hpi_details: 53F presenting with 15 watery stools/day, lower abdominal pain, leukocytosis (WBC 28,000), and C. diff toxin B positive following recent dental antibiotic therapy.
ideas: She thinks she contracted severe food poisoning from a restaurant seafood meal she ate over the weekend.
concerns: She is worried that she will pass out from severe dehydration and collapse while home alone.
expectations: She hopes to receive IV fluids for hydration and a strong anti-diarrheal medication so she can travel back home safely.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Clostridioides difficile Fulminant Colitis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Clostridioides difficile Fulminant Colitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes immediate cessation of the inciting antibiotic plus oral/rectal vancomycin (with adjunctive IV metronidazole for fulminant disease), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and high fever following clindamycin antibiotic course
Key HPI features: 53F presenting with 15 watery stools/day, lower abdominal pain, leukocytosis (WBC 28,000), and C. diff toxin B positive following recent dental antibiotic therapy.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.9C, HR 118, BP 98/62, RR 22 (hypotensive, tachycardic). Diffusely tender, distended abdomen with hypoactive bowel sounds; signs of dehydration. Bloods: WBC 28,000 /uL, Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (baseline 0.8, acute kidney injury), Lactate 2.8 mmol/L, Albumin 2.6 g/dL. Stool PCR/EIA confirms C. difficile toxin B. CT abdomen/pelvis shows diffuse colonic wall thickening ('accordion sign') and pericolonic fat stranding, without perforation or toxic megacolon. Meets IDSA criteria for fulminant C. difficile colitis (WBC > 15,000, rising creatinine, hypotension).
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Clostridioides difficile Fulminant Colitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Inflammatory bowel disease flare without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Very high stool frequency (>10-15/day) with high WBC — suggests fulminant/severe disease, risk of toxic megacolon.
management_principles: Immediately discontinue the inciting antibiotic (clindamycin) and start oral Vancomycin 500mg PO/NG QID plus a vancomycin retention enema (500mg in 100mL saline PR q6h) for fulminant disease; add IV Metronidazole 500mg q8h as an adjunct
Avoid antimotility agents (e.g., loperamide) and opioids, which can precipitate toxic megacolon
Obtain urgent surgical consultation for possible subtotal colectomy if perforation, toxic megacolon, worsening lactate, or clinical deterioration despite 24-48h of maximal medical therapy
Provide aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and electrolyte correction, with serial abdominal exams and repeat imaging to monitor for toxic megacolon or perforation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Clostridioides difficile Fulminant Colitis
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for severe watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and high fever following clindamycin antibiotic course
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for infectious_disease
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: Recent antibiotic use disrupts normal gut flora, allowing C. difficile to overgrow and produce toxin, causing profuse watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, and a dangerously elevated white cell count.
red_flags: Very high stool frequency (>10-15/day) with high WBC — suggests fulminant/severe disease, risk of toxic megacolon

must_ask.say: Have you taken any antibiotics in the past few weeks?
How many watery stools are you having per day?
Where is the abdominal pain, and how severe is it?
Have you had a fever with this?
How soon after starting the antibiotic did the diarrhea begin?

history.answer: Doctor, I have had terrible watery diarrhea and severe belly cramps for the past three days, and I am running a high fever.
It started about three days ago, right toward the end of an antibiotic course my dentist gave me, and it has gotten progressively worse.
I have about 15 bowel movements a day. It is completely watery, very foul-smelling, and not greasy.
I have not noticed any bright red blood, but there has been some slimy mucus mixed into the water.
Yes, it wakes me up multiple times every night with urgent cramping, so I can barely sleep.
I have intense cramping pain all across my lower belly. Passing stool does not really relieve it, and I constantly feel the urge to go again.
I have had high fevers and shaking chills since yesterday. I feel quite nauseated, but I haven't thrown up.
My mouth is parched and I feel very dizzy and faint when I stand up. I have barely passed any urine today because nothing stays in me.
I assumed I must have picked up a terrible case of food poisoning from some seafood I had a few days ago.
I have not traveled anywhere recently, nor have I gone camping or drunk untreated stream or well water.
I just completed a 7-day course of clindamycin three days ago for a tooth infection. I have not been admitted to any hospital recently.
I haven't had chronic weight loss, though I feel like I've dropped a few pounds over the last few days just from losing so much fluid.
No, it does not seem related to milk, dairy, bread, or any specific food.
No, my bowel habits were completely regular once a day until this started, and stress has never caused anything like this.
I have not had any painful or swollen joints, skin rashes, mouth ulcers, or red eyes.
My heart feels like it is beating fast because I am so dehydrated and feverish, but I do not have a history of heat intolerance, hand tremors, or facial flushing.
I assumed I must have picked up a terrible case of food poisoning from some seafood I had a few days ago.
With how often I'm rushing to the bathroom, I'm terrified I'll pass out from dehydration when nobody is around to help me.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol five years ago. I have no history of inflammatory bowel disease or kidney trouble.
I had my appendix removed with keyhole surgery about twenty years ago, but no other operations or hospital stays.
I take lisinopril 10 mg once every morning for blood pressure. I am not taking any over-the-counter pain pills, herbs, or antidiarrheal medicines.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only have a glass of wine on social occasions once or twice a month, and nothing since this illness began.
I work full-time as an accountant in an office, and I live with my husband in a house.
My father had high blood pressure and died of a stroke in his seventies. My mother is healthy, and nobody in my family has had colon cancer or Crohn's disease.
My last menstrual period was about two years ago when I went through menopause at age 51. There is no possibility of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Patient appears acutely ill, diaphoretic, flushed, and in evident distress from abdominal cramping.
Temperature 38.9°C, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, heart rate 118 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
Marked postural blood pressure drop with compensatory tachycardia and dizziness upon standing.
Mucous membranes are dry with cracked lips and reduced salivation; oropharynx is otherwise clear.
Decreased skin turgor with delayed recoil and capillary refill prolonged to 3 seconds; no rash or purpura.
Abdomen is moderately distended without visible peristalsis or caput medusae.
Hypoactive bowel sounds throughout all four abdominal quadrants; no bruits noted.
Diffuse tenderness across the abdomen, most prominent in the lower abdomen, without rigid involuntary guarding.
Liquid, foul-smelling stool coating the glove with no palpable rectal masses, fissures, or gross bleeding.
